docs.title: Country Projection Model (CPM) ToolUser Guide
docs.text: A step-by-step guide to setting up the CPM Tool, updating data, forecasting the external environment, and producing, reviewing and submitting a focus-economy forecast.

docs.title: What this guide covers
docs.text:
• Getting Started

    System requirements and setup of Python, Visual Studio Code and the cpm_venv virtual environment.

  • Concepts

    Economy groupings and linkages, the folder structure of the tool, and the three-stage forecasting process.

  • Forecasting Workflow

    Updating the datastore, running the external economies, configuring attributes.json, the model's nine steps, and applying judgment.

  • Hands-on Exercise

    A worked example for Bhutan, with both a one-shot run and a recommended manual run.

  • Reference

    Tips and common pitfalls, a command cheat sheet, a glossary, and a recap.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
This section explains how the CPM Tool is organised before you run it.

  • Economy Groupings and Linkages — which economies are modelled as the external environment and which are focus economies.
  • CPM Tool Structure — what each folder in the project does.
  • Forecasting Process — the three stages, from data update to the focus-economy forecast.

docs.title: Economy Groupings and Linkages
docs.text:
The CPM links each focus economy to a common external environment made up of four economies: the United States (US), the euro area, Japan and the People's Republic of China (PRC). Developing Asia economies are grouped by subregion, and Bhutan, India and the Philippines are the pilot economies.

Economy groupings and transmission links. Pilot economies are highlighted. Russia, and Australia and New Zealand, are shown as additional links.

docs.title: CPM Tool Structure
docs.text:
The project folder is organised into infrastructure modules and country modules.

Folder Role datastore_pumps Pulls external data datastore / datastore_api Stores and serves series model_infrastructure Builds and solves models reporting_infrastructure Produces charts and tables us · cn · jp · ea External environment models in · bt · ph Focus-country models

Country folder contents

Each country folder contains the scripts for the nine model steps, together with key files such as attributes.json, create_model.py and a data_files/ folder.

docs.title: Forecasting Process
docs.text:
A forecast round moves through three stages. Each stage depends on outputs saved to the datastore by the stage before it.

The three-stage forecasting process. Stage What happens Where 1. Update data Refresh the central datastore with the latest data datastore_pumps 2. Forecast external environment Run the US first, then the PRC, Japan and the euro area us, cn, jp, ea 3. Forecast focus economy Philippines and India can run in parallel. Bhutan depends on India due to currency peg. ph, in (and then bt)

docs.title: Hands-on Exercise
docs.text:
The exercise applies the full workflow to Philippines. Assume we are doing the October 2026 first round forecast.

Begin: Follow the steps below

docs.title: Step 1. Update data
docs.text:
Run datastore_pumps.update_all to refresh the datastore (see Forcasting Flow: Update Data).

python -m datastore_pumps.update_all

docs.title: Step 2. Forecast external economies.
docs.text:
Use this sample external economies forecast to tune the annual GDP growth.

Economy GDP growth 2026 GDP growth 2027 US 2.1 2.0 PRC 4.6 4.5 Euro area 0.8 1.2 Japan 0.7 0.8

docs.title: United States (us) forecast
docs.text:
1. Open and update the us/attributes.json

    {
    "forecast_id": "EX_OCT2026_F1",
    "forecast_end_period": "2027-Q4",
    "history_end_period": "2026-Q2",
    "history_start_period": "2010-Q1",
    "country_code": "US",
    "country_name": "United States"
}

  2. Quick run all required steps

    python -m us.run_all

  3. Update the GDP annual tunes

    1. In the windows explorer, open annual_tunes.csv (path = c:/CPM_Tool/us/tune_files/).

    2. In the roc4_ann_gdpw column, enter 1.021 (2026) and 1.020 (2027).

    3. Save and close the tune csv file.

  4. Run python -m us.simulate_forecast, to compute the forecast.

  5. Run python -m us.report_forecast, to generate the charts. Review the chart, once ok, proceed to the next step.

  6. Run python -m us.submit_forecast, to save the US forecast to the datastore/data.csv.

  3. Update the GDP annual tunes

    3. Save and close the tune csv file.

  4. Run python -m cn.simulate_forecast, to compute the forecast.

  5. Run python -m cn.report_forecast, to generate the charts. Review the chart, once ok, proceed to the next step.

  6. Run python -m cn.submit_forecast, to save the PRC forecast to the datastore/data.csv.

Repeat the process for euro area (ea) and Japan (jp).

docs.title: Step 3. Forecast Philippines
docs.text:
1. Open and update the ph/attributes.json

    {
    "external_forecast_id": "EX_OCT2026_F1",
    "forecast_id": "PH_OCT2026_F1",
    "forecast_end_period": "2027-Q4",
    "history_start_period": "2010-Q1",
    "country_code": "PH",
    "country_name": "The Philippines"
}

  2. This time, we will go through the nine steps. Run the commands one at a time.

    # First, configure forecast attributes in attributes.json
python -m ph.create_model
python -m ph.request_data
python -m ph.prepare_history

python -m ph.report_steady_calibration
#  review calibration, then continue

python -m ph.filter_history

python -m ph.report_filter
#  review filter results

python -m ph.simulate_forecast
#  apply judgmental adjustments

python -m ph.report_forecast
#  review forecast results, then submit

python -m ph.submit_forecast

Other focus economies

The same sequence applies to any country module — replace ph with the country code, for example in for the India.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Before running any forecast, prepare your computer so that the CPM Tool can run in its own Python environment.

  1. Check that your machine meets the System Requirements.
  2. Follow Installation and Setup to install the software

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Minimum Python Version 3.12 or later Code editor Microsoft Visual Studio Code Memory At least 8 GB of RAM

docs.title: Installation and Setup
docs.text: Follow these steps once on each computer that will run the CPM Tool.

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
1. Download and install Python 3.12 or later.
  2. Download and install Microsoft Visual Studio Code.

  3. Create a new folder in drive C and name it CPM_Tool.

  4. Extract CPM_tool.zip to C:/CPM_Tool.

  5. Open Visual Studio Code.

  6. Go to File › Open Folder, then select C:\CPM_Tool.

  7. Open terminal. Go to View › Terminal.

  8. Create the CPM tool Python environment. Enter the following command in the terminal:

    WindowsmacOS 
    python -m venv cpm_venv

    python3 -m venv cpm_venv

    Check the explorer

    Verify in the Visual Studio Code explorer that the cpm_venv directory now exists.

  9. Activate the environment. Enter the following command in the terminal:

    WindowsmacOS 
    cpm_venv\Scripts\activate

    source cpm_venv/bin/activate

    Activate first

    The terminal prompt should show (cpm_venv) before you install packages.

  10. Install the required Python packages listed in requirements.txt. Enter the following command in the terminal:

    WindowsmacOS 
    pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

    pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

    Python package dependencies docs/requirements.txt

    Check that all the packages listed below are installed in the cpm_venv\Lib\site-packages (for Windows) or cpm_venv/lib/python3.x/site-packages (for macOS) folder.

        timescroll >= 0.6.1
    macrotap >= 0.3.0
    datapie >= 0.6.3
    irispie-ce >= 0.79.5
    loguru
    ipython

  11. Test run. Enter the following command in the terminal:

    WindowsmacOS 
    python -m us.run_all

    python3 -m us.run_all

  12. Chart generation confirms that the setup is complete.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. Fails to Install daqp

    This error happens because pip is trying to compile the Python package daqp from source (building a wheel). This requires a C/C++ compiler and build tools (such as a C++ compiler or CMake) that are missing or not properly configured in your Windows PowerShell environment.

    Here is how to fix it.

    Install pre-built wheels or Microsoft C++ Build Tools

    The easiest way is to make sure pip can download a pre-compiled wheel, or to install the required build tools so it can compile.

    Step 1: Upgrade pip, setuptools and wheel

    First step

    Run the following command to make sure your package installers are up to date. This often allows pip to fetch compatible pre-compiled binaries:

    python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

    Verification

    Check that the output shows successfully updated versions of pip, setuptools and wheel.

    Step 2: Install Microsoft C++ Build Tools (if compilation is required)

    Alternative method

    If an up-to-date wheel isn't available for your Python version, you need the compiler toolchain:

    1. Download the Visual Studio Build Tools.
    2. During installation, select the workload "Desktop development with C++".

    3. Complete the installation and restart your terminal.

      Verification

      Run cl in PowerShell to check that the Microsoft C/C++ compiler is accessible in your path.

  2. Failed to activate environment cpm_venv

    This error occurs because PowerShell restricts running scripts by default for security reasons. The safest and easiest way to fix this is to change the execution policy for your current terminal session only.

    Step 1: Bypass the execution policy for the current session

    Recommended and least invasive

    Run this command in your PowerShell terminal to allow scripts to run in the current window:

    Set-ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Scope Process

    Verification

    Type Get-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process and confirm that it returns Unrestricted.

    Step 2: Activate the virtual environment

    Now run your activation command again:

    WindowsmacOS 
    cpm_venv\Scripts\activate

    source cpm_venv/bin/activate

    Verification

    Check that your terminal prompt now starts with (cpm_venv).

docs.title: Tips and Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Run from the root directory

    Always execute from the main directory so that the proper modules are used.

  • Respect the sequence

    Every step depends on the outputs of the one before it.

  • Review judgment

    simulate_forecast is where judgment is applied — revisit existing adjustments against current conditions.

  • Use the report steps

    Steps 4, 6 and 8 validate calibration, data quality and forecast reasonableness.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Term Meaning CPM Country Projection Model Datastore Central store of historical series and submitted forecasts, served through datastore_api External environment The US, euro area, Japan and PRC models whose forecasts feed the focus economies Focus economy A country forecast using the external environment (pilot: Bhutan, India, Philippines) Forecast ID Identifier for a forecast round; part of the datastore storage key Steady-state calibration The model's long-term equilibrium assumptions, reviewed in Step 4 Kalman filter / filtering Separates trends from cyclical components in historical data (Step 5) Tune A target value set directly for a variable; the simulation solves for the shocks needed to hit it Exogenize / endogenize Fix a variable at a set value / let a shock adjust freely so the target is met roc Gross rate of change (e.g. 1.05 = 5% growth) Real exchange rate gap Computed against the US dollar using US CPI projections — the reason the US runs first

Country codes: bt Bhutan · cn PRC · ea euro area · in India · jp Japan · ph Philippines · us United States

docs.title: Recap: From Data to Submitted Forecast
docs.text:
1. Set up the environment and run everything from the project root.
  2. Update and refresh the datastore with datastore_pumps.update_all.
  3. Build the external environment: US first, then CN, JP and EA.
  4. Run focus countries: PH, IN, and then BT.
  5. Work through the nine steps in order, pausing at the review gates.
  6. Apply judgment through annual tunes, then report and submit.

docs.title: Forecasting Workflow
docs.text:
This section walks through a full forecast round.

Always run from the project root and activate Python environment

Execute every command from the main project directory (for example C:\CPM_Tool) with cpm_venv activated, so that the correct modules are used.

WindowsmacOS 
cpm_venv\Scripts\activate

source cpm_venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Economy Forecast Order
docs.text:
For each forecast round, the external economies are forecast before the focus economies, and the United States runs first.

Why the US first?

US CPI projections are needed to compute real exchange rate gaps against the US dollar for all other external economies.

docs.title: Step 1: Manually update data
docs.text:
If you have data that is entered manually, update the CSV file before running update_all.

Ex. Bhutan's' data are updated manually before running update_all.

1. Get the source data. Download the latest Monthly Statistical Bulletin from the Royal Monetary Authority of Bhutan publications page: https://www.rma.org.bt/publication/31/

Source: Monthly Statistical Bulletin list on the RMA website.

2. Update the CSV file. Enter the new observations in datastore_pumps/manual/bhutan.csv. The file holds quarterly series (for example NGDP and RGDP) in one block and monthly series (for example CPI) in another.

Layout of datastore_pumps/manual/bhutan.csv — a quarterly block (NGDP, RGDP) and a monthly block (CPI).

3. Refresh the datastore. Save and close the file, then run python -m datastore_pumps.update_all.

Keep the existing layout

Add new periods below the last observation in each block and keep the existing headers and date formats (YYYY-Qn for quarterly, YYYY-MM for monthly).

Adding annual data

Add/insert __yearly__ column to store annual data. When adding a new CSV file, ensure that its filename is also added to this section 

    #%% Manual resources
    manual_resources = (
        "bhutan.csv", "china.csv",
    )

docs.title: Step 2: Run update_all.py
docs.text:
python -m datastore_pumps.update_all      # → datastore/data.csv

Connection errors when running update_all

update_all downloads data from online sources such as FRED and IMF. If the connection is slow or unstable, or a data provider is temporarily unavailable, the run may stop with a connection or timeout error.

If this happens, wait a few minutes, then run the command again.

If the error persists, check your internet connection or check the source website if it is down and try again later.

Sample Data Source Error

docs.title: How update_all.py works
docs.text:
1. data_source_info.csv defines the metadata-to-source map.
  2. Filtering by provider or resource creates relevant_map.
  3. Entries become request_strings; output_mapping links them to storage keys.
  4. macrotap pulls the data; manual_resources are read from .csv files.
  5. api.submit writes the datastore and renames variables.

docs.title: B: Configuring attributes.json
docs.text:
Each country model has an attributes.json file that sets the identifiers and sample periods for the forecast round. Review and update it before running the model.

What forecast IDs are for

Forecast IDs label each forecast round. They are part of the key under which results are saved in the datastore, so they let you:

  • Keep track of different forecast rounds, such as a January forecast, February forecast, etc., without mixing up results.
  • Properly link models to each other. A focus-country model uses the forecast IDs to find the right external economies inputs.

Agree on a naming standard before you start

Because forecast IDs are used to store and retrieve results across models, it is worth agreeing on a naming convention with your team before the first forecast round. A consistent standard IDs makes it easy to see which round a result belongs to and avoids linking a model to the wrong inputs.

Economy ID Format Example ID Note External economies EX_(MMMYYYY)_F(forecast round) EX_JAN2026_F1 All external economies should use the same forecast ID for each forecast round. That is, us ID should be the same in cn, ea, and jp. Focus economies (2-char country code)_(MMMYYYY)__F(forecast round) PH_JAN2026_F1

Whatever convention you choose, use it consistently across all country models, and keep a record of what each ID refers to.

Attributes Settings

Setting What it controls Applicable to Example us_forecast_id US unique identifier for this forecast round cn, ea, jp "EX_JAN2026_F1" forecast_id Unique identifier for this forecast round All "EX_JAN2026_F1" for cn, ea, jp/ PH_JAN2026_F1 for ph external_forecast_id External forecast set used by domestic models ph, in, bt "EX_JAN_F1" forecast_end_period End date for projections All "2027-Q4" history_end_period Last period of historical data us, cn, ea, jp "2025-Q4" history_start_period Start of historical sample All "2010-Q1"

Illustrative attributes.json

United States: us 

{
  "forecast_id": "EX_JAN2026_F1",
  "forecast_end_period": "2027-Q4",
  "history_end_period": "2026-Q2",
  "history_start_period": "2010-Q1"
}

For cn, ea, jp 

{
  "us_forecast_id": "EX_JAN2026_F1",
  "forecast_id": "EX_JAN2026_F1",
  "forecast_end_period": "2027-Q4",
  "history_end_period": "2026-Q2",
  "history_start_period": "2010-Q1"
}

For focus economies: ph, in, bt 

{
  "external_forecast_id": "EX_JAN2026_F1",
  "forecast_id": "PH_JAN2026_F1",
  "forecast_end_period": "2027-Q4",
  "history_start_period": "2010-Q1"
}

docs.title: The Model Nine Steps
docs.text:
Every country model follows the same nine steps, grouped into three phases: Phase A (Build and Load), Phase B (Calibrate and Filter), and Phase C (Forecast and Submit). Each step is a module run from the project root:

WindowsmacOS 
python -m {country}.{step}

python3 -m {country}.{step}

For example, python -m us.create_model runs Step 1 for United States.

The model nine steps, with review checkpoints and the judgment step.

Use the report steps

Steps 4, 6 and 8 validate calibration, data quality and forecast reasonableness. Pause at each one and review the outputs before moving on.

Quick run (all steps)Step by step

Use the run_all module in each country folder to skip report_steady_calibration and report_filter.

Note: Any applied tunes will refresh and revert to their original state once run_all is executed.

python -m us.run_all
python -m cn.run_all
python -m jp.run_all
python -m ea.run_all
python -m in.run_all
python -m bt.run_all

Use the step-by-step run when you need to review calibration and filter results.

python -m {country}.create_model
python -m {country}.request_data
python -m {country}.prepare_history
python -m {country}.report_steady_calibration
python -m {country}.filter_history
python -m {country}.review_filter
python -m {country}.simulate_forecast
python -m {country}.review_forecast
python -m {country}.submit_forecast

docs.title: Steps Description
docs.text: # Step Module What it does 1 Create Model create_model Creates and calibrates the economic model with country-specific parameters. Saves the model to a pickle file for use in later steps. 2 Request Data from Datastore request_data Requests historical data from the central datastore based on the input mapping configuration, and downloads the raw data needed for estimation and forecasting. 3 Prepare History prepare_history Processes raw historical data, applies transformations, calculates derived variables and prepares the dataset for running the Kalman filter on the history. 4 Review Steady-State Calibration report_steady_calibration Generates charts and analysis of the model's steady-state calibration against historical data. Review that long-term equilibrium assumptions are appropriate before filtering and forecasting. 5 Filter History filter_history Applies statistical filters to separate trends from cyclical components, creating the filtered series used as forecast inputs. 6 Report Filter report_filter Generates charts and analysis of the filtered data to validate the trend–cycle decomposition and review model inputs. 7 Simulate Forecast simulate_forecast Runs the model to generate forecasts. This is the step that typically requires manual, judgmental adjustments — see Simulate Forecast and Judgment. 8 Report Forecast report_forecast Creates charts, tables and analytical outputs presenting the forecast in a standard format for review and distribution. 9 Submit Forecast submit_forecast Uploads the forecast results to the central datastore, making them available to other models and for final reporting.

docs.title: Simulate Forecast and Judgment
docs.text: simulate_forecast (Step 7) is where judgment enters the forecast. There are two ways to apply it: annual tunes and manual adjustments.

docs.title: Annual Tunes
docs.text:
• Tunes set a variable directly; the simulation solves for the shocks needed to hit the target.
  • Tunes constrain the annual result — the model determines the quarterly path.
  • Enter annual values in tune_files/annual_tunes.csv where forecast_span = 1.
  • roc is the gross rate of change, and all rates, including interest rates, are entered as decimals.
  • Save and close the file before running the forecast.

Annual Tunes File

Entering rates

You want Enter 5% growth (as roc) 1.05 3% growth (as roc) 1.03 A 6.5% interest rate 0.065

How annual tunes work

docs.title: Quarterly tunes adjustments
docs.text:
The simulation script contains a free-form area for judgment on variables and shocks that are already declared in the model.

#==================================================================
# Add judgmental adjustments here

## Syntax
#   quick_tunes = {"<variable>": {ir.qq(<year>, <q>): <value>, ...}, ...}
# Set quarters and values with: ir.qq(2025, 4): 1.008
#   - one entry per quarter, several quarters go in the same inner dictionary
#   - quarter must be in the forecast period and have no actual data
#   - don't tune a quarter that is already pinned
#   - don't tune all 4 quarters of a year that also has an annual tune
# Variables available for quarterly tuning:
#   roc_gdp  gross Q/Q, 1.005 = 0.5% q/q   (lever: tune_gdp_gap, or shk_gdp_gap on old models)
#   roc_cpi  gross Q/Q, 1.008 = 0.8% q/q   (lever: tune_roc_cpi)
#   i        decimal, 0.0575 = 5.75%       (lever: tune_i)
#   e        level, same units as the data (lever: tune_e; not available for BT, e is pegged to IN)

quick_tunes = {
    #"roc_gdp": {ir.qq(2026,2): 1.05, ir.qq(2026,3): 1.006,},
    #"roc_cpi": {ir.qq(2026, 3): 1.02, },
    #"i": {ir.qq(2026, 3): 0.0575, },        
}

# Check which GDP lever is available
gdp_lever = "tune_gdp_gap" if "tune_gdp_gap" in shock_names else "shk_gdp_gap"

# Define levers
quick_levers = {"roc_gdp": gdp_lever, "roc_cpi": "tune_roc_cpi", "i": "tune_i", "e": "tune_e", }

# Sanity check ranges
quick_ranges = {"roc_gdp": (0.9, 1.1), "roc_cpi": (0.9, 1.1), "i": (0, 0.3), }

# Perform swap
for n, points in quick_tunes.items():
    for t, v in points.items():
        # Quarter must be in the forecast span
        if t not in forecast_span:
            raise ValueError(f"Quick tune: {n} in {t} is outside the forecast span")
        # Quarter must not already be pinned by actual available
        if n in history_db and history_db[n].end >= t:
            raise ValueError(f"Quick tune: {n} in {t} already has actual data")
        # Value must look like the right unit (Optional check if needed)
        lo, hi = quick_ranges.get(n, (-math.inf, math.inf))
        if not lo <= v <= hi:
            raise ValueError(f"Quick tune: {n} in {t} = {v} is outside {lo} to {hi}; check units")
        plan.swap_anticipated(t, (n, quick_levers[n]), )
        input_db[n][t] = v



#==================================================================

No new variables

New variables cannot be introduced here unless they are first added to the model equations.

Revisit existing judgment

Review adjustments carried over from earlier rounds against current conditions before re-running.
